section_titles: Assessment of VTE recurrence risk after acute PE
key_points: Assessment of VTE recurrence risk after acute PE is complex; carriers of some hereditary thrombophilias (deficiency of antithrombin, protein C, protein S, homozygous factor V Leiden, or homozygous prothrombin G20210A) are often candidates for indefinite anticoagulant treatment after a first PE occurring without a major reversible risk factor.

Testing for thrombophilia (including antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant) may be considered in patients with VTE at young age (e.g. <50 years) or with a strong family history to help tailor long-term anticoagulant regimen and dose.
No evidence of clinical benefit of extended anticoagulant treatment is currently available for carriers of heterozygous factor V Leiden or prothrombin 20210A mutation.
Meta-analyses of phase III studies showed approximately a 40% reduction in risk for major bleeding with NOACs compared with VKAs during the first 3–12 months of anticoagulant treatment.
Risk of major bleeding is highest in the first month of anticoagulant treatment, then declines and remains stable over time.

Bleeding risk factors include advanced age (particularly >75 years), previous bleeding, anaemia, active cancer, previous stroke, chronic renal or hepatic disease, concomitant antiplatelet or NSAID therapy, other serious acute or chronic illness, and poor anticoagulation control.

Bleeding risk should be assessed at initiation and reassessed periodically (e.g. annually for low-risk, every 3–6 months for high-risk patients) and used to identify and treat modifiable risk factors and to influence duration/regimen/dose of anticoagulant treatment after acute PE.
content.testing_considerations: Consider thrombophilia testing in patients with VTE at young age (<50 years) or without identifiable risk factors, especially with a strong family history; testing may include assays for antithrombin, protein C, protein S deficiencies and genetic testing for F5 (factor V Leiden) and F2 (prothrombin G20210A) variants. Note limited evidence to support extended anticoagulation for heterozygous carriers of F5 or F2 variants.
content.bleeding_risk_summary: Historical cohort studies reported high annual major bleeding with VKAs; NOACs reduce major bleeding risk (~40%) compared with VKAs in meta-analyses. Assess and periodically reassess bleeding risk and modify management accordingly.
recommendations: Individualize duration of anticoagulant therapy after PE based on presence of transient/reversible risk factors, patient age, thrombophilia status, and bleeding risk.
Use bleeding risk assessment (implicit judgement or formal score) at anticoagulation initiation and periodically thereafter to guide management.
